candidates.title: At Equal Inference Cost, Multi-Agent Structure Does Not Beat a Single Frozen Agent
candidates.citationVelocity: Semantic Scholar rate-limited (HTTP 429) after repeated attempts; paper is 0 days old per today's listing placement (abs page shows a Jun 25 submission date anomaly, see toolDegradation)
candidates.institution: Trinity College Dublin + University College Dublin + Dublin City University
communitySignals: No Papers with Code repo found
No public GitHub link found in the fetched full text
credibilityEvidence: Section VI: iso-call (total LLM-calls-fixed) controlled comparison on ALFWorld (n=134): single-agent executor evolution significantly beats unevolved baseline (+0.097, McNemar p=0.021); full Planner-Executor-Critic team attains highest mean (0.769) but is not statistically separable from the single agent (0.754, Delta=+0.015, p=0.80) despite spending 1.8x the evaluation calls (32.2 vs 18.0/task)
Section VII-A: per-role leave-one-in decomposition localizes all realized team value to the Executor (LOI:exec +0.075); Planner-only arm does not separate from Stock (+0.067, p=0.15)
Section VII-B: both budget regimes reported -- even under the team-favoring env-rollouts regime granting 2-3x free compute, the team only ties the single agent (0.739=0.739)

Section VII-C: instrumented collapse-and-starvation mechanism -- Planner and Critic prompts evolve to empty (froze empty across every clean run) because a frozen 7B backbone has no role-differentiation headroom
Second benchmark (WebShop, n=80, dense reward): evolution is null for the single agent (0.245 approx Stock 0.242) and the team trends worse (0.185, Delta=-0.060 vs single, p=0.12)

Limitations section explicitly self-scopes to: single frozen 7B backbone, one topology (Planner-Executor-Critic only), one optimizer (coordinate ascent), two benchmarks, single-greedy task-as-unit bootstrap, and an incomplete env-rollouts LOI decomposition (a documented KeyError in one cell)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Two independent budget regimes, a per-role leave-one-in decomposition, McNemar significance tests with bootstrap CIs, and an instrumented mechanism (role collapse + call starvation) together support the narrow claim; the paper itself scopes the conclusion to a frozen 7B backbone and does not claim it transfers to larger or heterogeneous models.
reproducibilityEvidence: Full architecture, algorithm, per-cell hyperparameters, and the evolved executor prompt text are published in the paper and appendices
No public code repository link found in the fetched full text
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The claim 'on a frozen backbone at equal inference cost, multi-agent structure adds cost without a corresponding benefit' is supported by two benchmarks, two budget regimes, and a mechanism-level explanation, not a single headline number.
candidates.primaryLimitation: All results use one frozen 7B backbone and one Planner-Executor-Critic topology; whether role-differentiation headroom (and thus multi-agent value) emerges with larger or heterogeneous backbones is explicitly left untested.
candidates.presentationReason: Iso-call invariant, three budget meters, per-role decomposition, and limitations are each stated precisely with explicit statistical procedures (McNemar tests, bootstrap CIs).
candidates.reason: Directly challenges the default assumption behind most production multi-agent frameworks (CrewAI, AutoGen, LangGraph-style planner/executor/critic pipelines) with a controlled, budget-fair comparison and a mechanistic explanation for why the extra roles fail to pay -- the single strongest capability/limits candidate in today's batch.

candidates.title: Does Your Agent's Memory Survive a Model Upgrade? A Controlled Study of Memory Portability
candidates.citationVelocity: Semantic Scholar rate-limited (HTTP 429) after repeated attempts; published 5 days ago (submitted 2026-09-04)
communitySignals: No Papers with Code repo found
credibilityEvidence: Section 3.5: four hypothesis tests (H1, H2, H4a, H7a) fixed before data collection in a signed Git tag (hypothesis-lock-v1), independently verifiable via 'git verify-tag'; the paper honestly reports that only 2 of 4 preregistered tests cleared the preregistered 5pp action threshold (H2, H7a), not all 4

Table 3: KG-fixed accuracy changes by only +0.0004 +/- 0.0020 following a writer swap (own-store 0.845-0.988), while NOTES shifts asymmetrically by +9.91pp (Llama-reading-Qwen) or -13.28pp (Qwen-reading-Llama) depending on migration direction

Embedding-migration test (E3): a 50/50 mixed index captures only 4.96 of the 11.90-point accuracy gain from full re-embedding, with an explicit sanity check confirming the two embedding spaces are genuinely different (cross-space cosine 0.904, below a 0.999 identity threshold) before counting the result

Diagnostic decomposition (E4): attributes 80% (0.467 +/- 0.014) of the NOTES accuracy deficit to information lost during initial construction (not reading), and 81% (0.364 +/- 0.012) of the RAG deficit to retrieval failure

Repair test (E6): store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach a 90% recovery target in all 48 test cases, while retaining raw source history enables recovery in 34 of 48 cases for one migration direction

Extensive self-disclosed methodology QA: docs/deviations.md logs every change with checksums, four implementation bugs caught before main runs via calibration checks, and three run-control bugs found and fixed during the repair experiment (E6), each documented rather than silently corrected
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Preregistration with a verifiable signed tag, honest reporting of 2-of-4 hypotheses missing the preregistered threshold, and a causal decomposition of loss by pipeline stage (construction vs. retrieval vs. reading) together support the format-comparison claims; the paper itself states this is a single cross-family migration pair (Llama <-> Qwen, both sub-10B) and not a sample of all model upgrades.
reproducibilityEvidence: Preregistration git tag, deviations log, and statistical code (standard-library only) are described as 'stored with the repository'
No public GitHub URL found in the fetched full text
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The core claims (fixed-schema KG-fixed transfers reliably; compressed NOTES are model-coupled and direction-asymmetric; partial embedding migration forfeits most of the re-embedding gain; raw-history retention materially improves repairability) are each backed by a dedicated controlled test with reported confidence intervals, and the paper explicitly narrows its own claim scope where results were mixed.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Tests a single cross-family model-upgrade pair (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct <-> Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M, both under 10B parameters) on 48 synthetic histories; generalization to larger models, same-family upgrades, or production-scale memory stores is untested.
candidates.presentationReason: Four memory formats, four migration tests, and the preregistration/deviation protocol are each defined precisely, with a dedicated 'lessons for a trustworthy migration test' section separating what was planned from what was found during execution.
candidates.reason: Addresses a concrete, underexamined operational risk for every team running a production memory layer (Mem0/Zep/Letta/LangMem-style stores) -- a routine model swap can silently degrade retrieval-dependent memory with no error raised -- backed by unusually rigorous preregistered methodology and a stage-level loss decomposition that turns into a direct design playbook.

candidates.title: Why Better Models Can Create Riskier Systems: Evidence from LLM Agents in Financial Markets
candidates.citationVelocity: Semantic Scholar rate-limited (HTTP 429) after repeated attempts; published 6 days ago (submitted 2026-09-03)
candidates.institution: MIT (EECS + Sloan School of Management) + Harvard Kennedy School (Belfer Center); senior author Andrew W. Lo (MIT Sloan, known for the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis and systemic-risk research)
communitySignals: No Papers with Code repo found (authors state code 'will be distributed with a repository license')
credibilityEvidence: Section 4.1 (RQ1): controlled panel of 7 LLMs x 64 scenarios (5 samples/scenario) with per-model OLS residualization against the fundamental price gap; pairwise non-corrective correlation regressed on capability score is significant under both ELO (t=3.94, p=0.001, R^2=0.475) and MMLU-Pro (t=4.88, p<0.001, R^2=0.580), while shared-provider is not significant (p=0.39/0.28) -- ruling out the simpler 'same company = same behavior' explanation

Empirical bootstrap (N=2 to 8 models, resampled with replacement) confirms a non-diversifiable risk floor (rho*sigma_r^2=0.010) closely tracks the theoretical AR(1) prediction, ruling out a small-sample artifact

Section 4.2 (RQ2): market simulation across 3 model families (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite) with noise traders and a market maker, 5 seeds/condition; LLM participation improves price discovery monotonically, and cross-model variation is explained by a single behavioral parameter (gap-sensitivity lambda)

Section 4.3 (RQ3): adding a shared adversarial misinformation stream (vs. a neutral-sentiment control) inverts the RQ2 finding -- tracking error rises 5-7x baseline at full LLM participation, directional accuracy collapses to 42-68% (one model below chance), because the induced errors are fully correlated rather than diversified away

Section 6 Discussion and Limitations explicitly state: all evidence comes from a simplified single-asset simulated market with exogenous fundamentals; real markets have correlated assets, endogenous liquidity, and strategic adaptation the study does not model; whether the same dynamics generalize to non-financial domains is stated as an open empirical question rather than implied
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Three separate, purpose-designed research questions (correlation-vs-capability regression, participation-scaling simulation, adversarial-information stress test) each with matched controls and significance testing support the capability-paradox claim within the tested financial-market simulation; the paper explicitly declines to claim the mechanism generalizes beyond that setting.
reproducibilityEvidence: Full simulation mechanics, decomposition equations, and capability benchmarks are specified in the paper and appendices
Authors state code will be released but no public repository link was found in the fetched text at time of review
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The 'capability paradox' claim (more capable models can increase, not decrease, correlated systemic risk) is supported by a significant regression, a bootstrap-validated risk-floor derivation, and a stress test showing the mechanism's downside, not a single anecdote.
candidates.primaryLimitation: All empirical evidence comes from a simplified simulated single-asset market with exogenous fundamentals; real markets' correlated assets, endogenous liquidity, and strategic adaptation could amplify or dampen the documented effect, and cross-domain generalization is explicitly untested.
candidates.presentationReason: The action decomposition (corrective vs. non-corrective), the risk-floor derivation, and each research question's setup/result/mechanism are stated precisely, with a dedicated Limitations paragraph and an appendix generalizing the framework to a second domain (insurance billing) as illustration rather than additional evidence.
candidates.reason: MIT/Harvard team with a named systemic-risk expert (Andrew W. Lo) formalizes and empirically tests a genuinely counterintuitive mechanism -- capability improvements can increase correlated, non-diversifiable systemic risk in multi-agent deployments -- with a significant regression, a validated theoretical risk floor, and a concrete failure demonstration under shared misinformation, directly relevant to anyone deploying frontier models at scale in agent fleets.
